title: Sioux City Ghosts Vintage Inspired Wool Ballcap
body_html:
PAYING HOMAGE TO THE FAST-PITCH SOFTBALL GREATS THE SIOUX CITY GHOSTS

History: What started as a boys club in a historically Black neighborhood in Sioux City, Iowa evolved into a barnstorming fast-pitch softball team that toured all over the nation. The Sioux City Ghosts were both elite players and comedic performers, playing “shadowball,” embarrassing the umpires, or playing in slow-motion to get the crowd going. Along with teams like the Harlem Globetrotters, their skill and showmanship made them a top attraction during the Great Depression, and they earned a permanent spot in Sioux City’s history books.

The Ghosts used a few different versions of a skull and crossbones logo, including this one, taken from a vintage souvenir program given out at one of their exhibition games. This ballcap is made with genuine wool broadcloth and a green satin underbrim and features a felt patch of the skull design worn by the Sioux City Ghosts.

The team's prowess soon made them one of the top touring attractions during the Great Depression, along with teams like the House of David and Harlem Globetrotters. After becoming widely known in the Midwest, the team toured California, the West, and Canada. As entertainment was an integral part of the appeal of these barnstorming teams, the Ghosts relied on comedy routines and displays of baseball skill like "Shadowball" to widen their appeal.

History: The Taiyo Cubs emerged from the vibrant Japanese American baseball culture of the Pacific Northwest in 1928. The club grew from Portland’s Taiyo Athletic Club, whose teams brought together younger players from several local sandlot clubs. That same year, the Dearborn Huskies joined the organization under the Taiyo Cubs name. At its peak in the 1930s, the broader Taiyo organization had around 120 members and fielded teams in baseball, football and basketball. These clubs helped create a sporting community for Japanese Americans at a time when segregation sharply limited access to established leagues.

Managed by player-manager Kazuto Tsuruoka, Nankai went 66–49–5 to finish second behind the Mainichi Orions. The club was already laying the foundation for a remarkable decade: just one year later, the Hawks went 72–24–8, the best winning percentage in NPB history at the time, and reached the Japan Series for the first time. Outfielder Makoto Kozuru was the club’s standout, batting .361 to lead the league and earning Best Nine honors. Among its most important young players was Michio Nishizawa, who had joined the team at just 15 years old in 1936. title: Shochiku Robins 1950 Authentic Wool Home Jersey
body_html:
AUTHENTIC WOOL HOME JERSEY HONORING THE 1950 SHOCHIKU ROBINS

History: The Shochiku Robins exploded onto the scene in 1950, the inaugural season of Japan’s new two-league professional structure. They won the Central League with a remarkable 98–35–4 record, led by MVP Makoto Kozuru, who hit .355 with 51 home runs and 161 RBI. Pitcher Juzo Sanada went 39–12 and won the inaugural Sawamura Award. The Robins advanced to the first-ever Japan Series, where they faced the Mainichi Orions and lost four games to two. Their spectacular debut remains one of the most remarkable seasons by a short-lived Japanese franchise.

title: Tokio Senators 1936 Authentic Wool Road Jersey
body_html:
AUTHENTIC WOOL ROAD JERSEY HONORING THE 1936 TOKIO SENATORS

History: The Tokio Senators were created in January 1936 as one of the founding clubs of Japan’s first professional baseball league. Backed by Seibu Railway and politician Arima Yoriyasu, the team was conceived as a Tokyo rival to the newly established Giants. Their home was Kamiigusa Stadium, a substantial new ballpark in western Tokyo. The Senators became known for their distinctive uniforms and aggressive style, but their existence was brief: after several name changes, the franchise was merged with the Nagoya Kinko team in 1941. Its legacy continued through players who later helped form another Senators club after World War II.

Made with authentic wool baseball flannel with felt appliqué lettering, this is a reproduction of the away jersey worn by the 1936 Tokio Senators.

They spent their first years barnstorming across the country, sometimes playing doubleheaders in different states on successive days, before joining the Negro National League in 1936 and eventually playing their home games at Yankee Stadium when the American League Yankees were on the road. Hall of Famer Satchel Paige had a stint with the Black Yankees, as did memorable stars like “Fats” Jenkins, Ted “Double Duty” Radcliffe, and “Mule” Suttles.

HEAVYWEIGHT PULLOVER HOODIE HONORING THE 1941 SEATTLE RAINIERS

History: In 1941, the Seattle Rainiers won their third straight Pacific Coast League pennant — the capstone of the greatest run in franchise history. Owner Emil Sick had bought the team just three years earlier, renamed them after his Rainier Brewing Company, built Sicks' Stadium in Rainier Valley, and watched his club win in 1939, 1940, and 1941 in succession. The Rainiers led all of minor league baseball in attendance across that stretch, packing the stadium beneath the shadow of Mount Rainier on summer nights that Seattle still talks about.

Made from our soft, heavyweight French terry and finished with embroidered felt lettering, this pullover hoodie honors the 1941 Seattle Rainiers with a design inspired by their home uniform.

History: The 1959 Salt Lake City Bees were a Pittsburgh Pirates affiliate playing at Derks Field, and they were very good — finishing 85-69 to win the PCL pennant by one and a half games over Vancouver, the first title in the club's history. Pitcher Dick Hall led the staff with an 18-4 record and a 1.87 ERA. Outfielder R.C. Stevens led the club with 19 home runs. It was the Bees' second year back in the Pacific Coast League after a long run in the Pioneer League, and they announced their return by winning the whole thing.

Made from genuine wool broadcloth with our signature green satin underbrim, this hat is inspired by the on-field ballcap worn by the 1959 Salt Lake City Bees.

History: In 1941, the Seattle Rainiers won their third straight Pacific Coast League pennant — the capstone of the greatest run in franchise history. Owner Emil Sick had bought the team just three years earlier, renamed them after his Rainier Brewing Company, built Sicks' Stadium in Rainier Valley, and watched his club win in 1939, 1940, and 1941 in succession. The Rainiers led all of minor league baseball in attendance across that stretch, packing the stadium beneath the shadow of Mount Rainier on summer nights that Seattle still talks about.

PCL president Clarence "Pants" Rowland used that energy to petition the major leagues for recognition as a third major league. The request was denied, but the Angels kept packing the house anyway, doing LA proud over a decade before the city would get its own big-league squad.

The Seals went out the right way — winning 101 games, taking the pennant two days before the season ended, and clinching the last championship of their 54-year history. History: The Hollywood Stars moved into Gilmore Field in 1939 — a brand-new park on Beverly Boulevard, next door to a CBS studio and across town from their rivals, the PCL's Los Angeles Angels. In their second year at Gilmore, the Stars went 84-94 and finished sixth — a below-.500 team playing in a park that belonged to Hollywood's most glamorous era. Bing Crosby, Gary Cooper, and Cecil B. DeMille were part of the ownership group. On a good night, they were in the stands too. The Stars would later grow into a championship team, winning three pennants before 1958, but everyone in Hollywood has to start somewhere.

Made from breathable knit mesh with tackle twill appliqué lettering and logos, this jersey is inspired by the home uniform worn by the 1940 Hollywood Stars.

title: Hollywood Stars 1957 Cotton Twill Ballcap
body_html:
COTTON TWILL BALLCAP HONORING THE 1957 HOLLYWOOD STARS

History: The 1957 Hollywood Stars played their last season at Gilmore Field knowing the end was near — the Dodgers were heading west, and that meant the PCL's Los Angeles clubs were finished. The Twinks, as they were affectionately called, went out swinging: 94 wins, third in the PCL, with future big leaguers Dick Stuart and Bill Mazeroski on the roster. On September 5, 1957, the final out was recorded at Gilmore Field. The stadium came down a year later. CBS Television City now sits on the land where Hollywood played its last game.

Made from sturdy cotton twill with our signature green satin underbrim, this hat is inspired by the on-field ballcap worn by the 1957 Hollywood Stars.

body_html:

History: The Los Angeles Angels played the 1942 season with the war hanging over everything. Pearl Harbor had come just months before Opening Day, and the PCL pushed on while rosters began to thin — players departing for military service as the summer wore on. The Angels, a Cubs affiliate playing at LA's Wrigley Field, finished just one game out of first place under manager Jigger Statz, their closest brush with a pennant in nearly a decade. They wouldn't get another chance until the war was over.

Made from breathable knit mesh with tackle twill appliqué lettering and logos, this jersey is inspired by the away uniform worn by the 1942 Los Angeles Angels.

title: Los Angeles Angels (PCL) 1957 Mesh V-Neck Home Jersey
body_html:
V-NECK MESH JERSEY HONORING THE 1957 LOS ANGELES ANGELS OF THE PCL

History: Steve Bilko — the Angels' top slugger, nicknamed the Babe Ruth of the PCL — had a publicist keep meticulous count of how often his name appeared in the Los Angeles papers. "There wasn't a movie star that could touch him," the publicist once said. By 1957, Bilko had won three straight PCL MVP awards and was the biggest celebrity in town — a 6-foot-1, 240-pound first baseman who hit 56 home runs that season, drove in 140, and played out his final year with the Angels as the Dodgers were packing up to leave Brooklyn. The major leagues were coming to Los Angeles, which meant the end of the line for the PCL Angels. They went out with Bilko, still swinging.

Made from breathable knit mesh with tackle twill appliqué lettering and logos, this jersey is inspired by the home uniform worn by the 1957 Los Angeles Angels.

title: Seattle City Series Wool Ballcap

That's what we had on our mind when we designed the City Series: a collection of hats that pulls subtle inspiration from a few iconic teams, but puts the town itself front and center.

This Seattle hat is made from genuine wool broadcloth, embroidered lettering, and our signature green satin underbrim.

title: Seattle Rainiers 1950 Authentic Wool Ballcap

The following year, with Hall of Famer Rogers Hornsby in the dugout and a five-tool dynamo named Jungle Jim Rivera in the outfield, the Rainiers would win the pennant. But 1950 was the year before all that — the year Seattle just came out to watch baseball.

Made from genuine wool broadcloth with our signature green satin underbrim, this hat is a recreation of the on-field ballcap worn by the 1950 Seattle Rainiers.

The Hall of Fame second baseman — .358 career average, two Triple Crowns — ran the club his way, and the Rainiers responded. Led by outfielder Jungle Jim Rivera, Seattle went 99-68 and won the PCL pennant, the franchise's first championship since their wartime trifecta of 1940, 1941, and 1942.

title: Seattle Rainiers 1955 Mesh V-Neck Home Jersey
body_html:
V-NECK MESH JERSEY HONORING THE 1951 SEATTLE RAINIERS

History: In 1955, with the Rainiers coming off a fifth-place finish and the franchise teetering, general manager Dewey Soriano made a phone call to his old Franklin High School teammate Fred Hutchinson, who was in a contract dispute with the Detroit Tigers. Hutchinson turned down Detroit and the Baltimore Orioles to come home and manage Seattle instead. The city responded like he'd never left: fans flooded back to Sicks' Stadium, and Hutchinson guided the Rainiers to a 95-77 record and the PCL pennant — the last championship of the Emil Sick era, won by a Seattle boy who came home when it mattered.

Made from breathable knit mesh with tackle twill appliqué lettering and logos, this jersey is inspired by the home uniform worn by the 1955 Seattle Rainiers

title: The Clemente Museum x Ebbets Field Short Sleeve Graphic T-Shirt
body_html:

History: On July 24, 1970 — just eight days after Three Rivers Stadium opened its doors — the Pittsburgh Pirates filled their brand-new ballpark with 43,290 fans to honor their star player, Roberto Clemente. Families flew in from Puerto Rico to see him play. There was a life-size wax figure of him on the field. And at the end of the evening, when the crowd wanted to shower him with gifts, Clemente asked them to donate the money to the Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh instead. Decades later in 2002, the MLB decided to designate September 15th as the league-wide Roberto Clemente day, timed to Hispanic Heritage Month.

In honor of the man himself, that historic 1970 celebration, as well as the day we currently set aside to honor him, we designed this 100% cotton graphic tee with a screen-printed design inspired by fliers and patches from the original Roberto Clemente Day on July 24, 1970

title: The Clemente Museum x Ebbets Field V-Neck Mesh Jersey
body_html:
MESH JERSEY MADE IN COLLABORATION WITH THE ROBERTO CLEMENTE MUSEUM

History: Long before he was a Hall of Famer, Roberto Clemente was a kid from Puerto Rico who fell in love with baseball on a neighborhood field. He never forgot that. Throughout his career he ran youth clinics across the island, and in Río Piedras — where he lived and raised his family — he coached and sponsored a local youth team, wearing an orange jersey with a custom script that nobody outside his neighborhood ever saw. That is, until 1994 when Clemente Museum founder Duane Rieder found it in the family home and took a quick photo. We partnered with The Clemente Museum to bring that unique design to a new collection honoring the eternal legacy of Roberto Clemente.

Made from breathable knit mesh and finished with tackle twill appliqué lettering, this jersey takes direct inspiration from the one found in Clemente's archive — from the color to the script to the stripes on the sleeve.

title: Charleston Charlies Pillbox Cap
body_html:
VINTAGE-STYLE WOOL PILLBOX HAT HONORING THE CHARLESTON CHARLIES

History: The Charleston Charlies were a Triple-A club in the International League from 1971 to 1983, playing at Watt Powell Park and cycling through four big league parents over their 13-year run. They won the league championship in 1977 — the same year they absorbed a handful of Toronto Blue Jays prospects on loan while the expansion club got its footing. Willie Randolph came through on his way to becoming a six-time All-Star. In their final season, 1983, the Charlies went 74-66 and made the playoffs one last time before the Indians moved the franchise to Maine.

Made from genuine wool broadcloth with felt appliqué lettering, this pillbox-style hat is a reproduction of the Charleston Charlies' on-field ballcap from 1983. The style first had its heyday in the late 1800s, but in 1976 the Pittsburgh Pirates helped bring the look back for a while. As a Pirates affiliate team, the Charlies adopted the look, and kept the pillbox as a part of their uniform after moving to Cleveland's farm system, where they swapped in the Indians' red and blue.

title: Milwaukee Brewers (AA) 1905 Pillbox Cap

VINTAGE-STYLE WOOL PILLBOX HAT HONORING THE MILWAUKEE BREWERS (AA)

History: In 1905, the Milwaukee Brewers put together one of the strongest seasons of the early American Association, winning 91 games against 59 losses and finishing second behind the Columbus Senators. Managed by “Pongo Joe” Cantillon, the Brewers drew 185,000 fans to Athletic Park, then Milwaukee’s baseball ground at Eighth and Burleigh. Quait Bateman led the lineup with a .314 average, and Tom Dougherty shouldered the heaviest pitching load, appearing in 45 games and winning 22. It was Milwaukee baseball in its early-20th-century form: long seasons, iron-armed pitchers and packed afternoons at the ballpark.

Made from genuine wool broadcloth with felt appliqué lettering, this hat calls back to the pillbox-style ballcaps popular around the turn of the 20th century. Back then, there wasn't a uniform style across all of pro baseball, and teams like the 1905 Milwaukee Brewers took the field with some unique looks — like this pillbox cap with the logo on the brim.

title: Phoenix Giants 1983 Pillbox Cap

VINTAGE-STYLE WOOL PILLBOX HAT HONORING THE PHOENIX GIANTS

The Phoenix Giants were the top affiliate in the Giants' system from 1966 through 1985, sitting in the Triple-A Pacific Coast League just one phone call away from Candlestick Park. The club won the PCL championship in 1977, and over the years sent a steady stream of talent up to San Francisco — making Phoenix one of the most reliable stops on the road to the big leagues.

Made from genuine wool broadcloth with felt appliqué lettering, this pillbox-style hat is a reproduction of the Phoenix Giants' on-field ballcap from 1983. The style first had its heyday in the late 1800s, but in 1976 the Pittsburgh Pirates helped bring the look back for a while. With its horizontal stripes and old-english 'P,' the Giants ballcap is a nod to the look the Pirates won the World Series with in 1979.

By the time Cozza retired after 32 seasons, he'd led Yale to 10 Ivy League championships and 179 wins, earning himself a spot in the College Football Hall of Fame as the winningest coach in Ivy League history. He never coached a bowl game or recruited five-star prospects. He just kept winning, quietly, in New Haven, for three decades.

Made from sturdy cotton twill and finished with our signature green satin underbrim, this ballcap honors Yale University

title: Texas A&M Sarge Cotton Twill Ballcap

History: In 1939, the Texas A&M Aggies didn't just win the Southwest Conference — they ran the table, finishing 11-0 with six shutouts and outscoring their opponents 198 to 18 over the regular season. Fullback John Kimbrough was the engine of the offense, and he saved his best for the Sugar Bowl — carrying the ball 25 times for 159 yards and two touchdowns in a 14-13 comeback win over Tulane that sealed the national championship. It remains the only consensus national title in program history, built on one of the most dominant defensive seasons college football had ever seen.

Made from sturdy cotton twill with our signature green satin underbrim, this ballcap honors Texas A&M University and "Sarge," a square-jawed, no-nonsense sergeant who, since appearing in a Battalion Humor Magazine comic strip in 1938, has become an enduring symbol of A&M's Corps of Cadets.

title: Harvard University Collard Crewneck Sweatshirt
body_html:
COLLARED CREWNECK SWEATSHIRT HONORING HARVARD UNIVERSITY

History: With 42 seconds left in the 1968 season finale, Yale led Harvard 29-13 and had the Ivy League title all but sewn up. What followed has never been forgotten. Harvard scored two touchdowns and converted two two-point conversions in the final seconds to tie the game 29-29 — and the Harvard Crimson's headline the next morning said everything: "Harvard Beats Yale, 29-29." The Crimson finished 8-0-1, shared the Ivy title, and produced one of the most celebrated moments in college football history.

Made from heavyweight cotton with a knit collar and felt appliqué lettering, this sweatshirt is inspired by retro looks which wandered Harvard Yard in the '70s and '80s.

title: Harvard University Cotton Varsity Cardigan
body_html:
VARSITY CARDIGAN SWEATER HONORING HARVARD UNIVERSITY

History: The varsity letter started at Harvard. In 1865, the baseball team began embroidering an Old English "H" on their gray flannel jerseys — and for the next 25 years, the captain would award those jerseys to players who competed in the biggest games of the season. You earned the H, or you gave it back. By the 1880s, the tradition had evolved into the lettersweater — a white knit with a crimson H, first worn by the crew team and soon adopted across every Harvard sport. This cardigan is a direct descendant of that tradition, one of the oldest in American athletics.

Made with a substantial cotton yarn and a felt 'H' patch, this cardigan sweater honors a historic institution and their legacy in modern sportswear that stretches back a century and a half.

body_html:

History: Harvard soccer has been played since 1905, and the program won its first national titles before the NCAA tournament even existed — claiming four Intercollegiate Soccer Football League championships between 1913 and 1930. The modern peak came in the mid-1980s, when the Crimson reached back-to-back College Cups in 1986 and 1987, advancing to the national semifinals both years. It remains the high-water mark for Harvard soccer, a two-year run that put the Crimson among the elite programs in the country.

Designed after vintage Crimson goalie uniforms, this collared long-sleeve jersey is made from a heavyweight 100% cotton jersey and finished with flocked lettering.

History: Harvard baseball has been played since 1865 — back when the flat-crowned pillbox was the standard cap in the game, players wore wool from head to toe, and the rules themselves were still being written. In 1877, a Harvard player named James Tyng became the first catcher to ever wear a mask behind the plate, after teammate Fred Thayer adapted a fencing mask to protect his face. It was a small invention with enormous consequences — and it happened in Cambridge, on a Harvard diamond.

The Alacranes were part of a golden era when Cuban ballparks welcomed elite talent from the Caribbean, Negro Leagues, and American professional baseball, making every winter game a showcase of international baseball at its highest level.

Their first era arrived in the late 1930s, when the team quickly established itself as a powerhouse, winning the 1939 championship behind legendary player-manager Lázaro Salazar. Playing in Santo Domingo’s young professional baseball era, Escogido finished 35–18 before meeting the Águilas Cibaeñas in a seven-game championship battle. Managed by Frank Genovese, the club combined Dominican talent with experienced players from across the Caribbean baseball world, delivering the first of three straight league titles. The victory marked the beginning of an era when the red uniforms of Escogido became a symbol of Dominican baseball excellence.

History: By 1953, the Estrellas Orientales had spent more than four decades representing San Pedro de Macorís, a city whose sugar mills and ballfields produced generations of gifted players. The club competed in the Dominican League's summer era, when weekend games unfolded under the Caribbean sun and rivalries with Licey, Escogido, and Águilas drew devoted crowds from across the island. The standings offered little reward that year, but the foundation was already in place for the Estrellas' long-awaited championship in 1954.

Sharing the ballpark with their crosstown rivals, los Diablos Rojos, the Tigres helped establish one of Mexican baseball's enduring rivalries, with alternating home dates turning the same grandstand into two entirely different worlds.

The Diablos Rojos finished 53–25 to claim the league title behind manager Lázaro Salazar, while Hall of Fame shortstop Willie Wells brought his trademark smooth fielding and powerful bat to the heart of the lineup. Across the league, legends like Josh Gibson, Martín Dihigo, and Ray Dandridge were filling ballparks, making that summer in Mexico City one of the richest concentrations of baseball talent anywhere in the world.

History: The 1950–51 Ponce Leones played under Hall of Famer Rogers Hornsby, who brought his famously demanding style to Puerto Rico after decades as one of baseball's greatest hitters. Ponce finished the winter campaign 43–35, staying in contention behind a veteran roster that reflected the island's growing importance in professional baseball. The season captured a moment when major league stars, Negro League veterans, and Puerto Rican standouts regularly shared the same diamond, making every night at Ponce a meeting point for baseball's many worlds.

History: Founded in 1935, the Universidad Autónoma de Guadalajara became one of Mexico’s most recognizable private universities and built a proud athletic tradition in Jalisco. Its athletic teams adopted the name Tecolotes, or owls — an identity which decades later became best known through the university’s football club, but the crest itself remains tied to the spirit of UAG athletics: a distinctive mark of a school founded during a transformative era in Mexican education and sport.

title: Xalapa Chileros 1963 Authentic Wool Ballcap

History: Xalapa, Veracruz claims to be the city where baseball first came to Mexico. Legend has it American soldiers introduced the game there during the Mexican-American War in 1847. When la Liga Invernal Veracruzana (the Veracruz Winter League) was founded in 1952, the Chileros became Xalapa's professional club — battling intense rivalries and riling up their home crowd for one memorable decade. The Chileros folded along with the league in 1963, but when the league was revived in '05, the green and white emerged from the history books ready to play ball, winning the championship in the 2007-08 season.

History: On April 18, 1981, Wade Boggs was playing third base for the Pawtucket Red Sox when the game against the Rochester Red Wings simply refused to end. Thirty-three innings, eight hours and twenty-five minutes, suspended in the early morning hours and resumed two months later — the longest professional baseball game ever played. Boggs was there for all of it. That same season, he led the International League in batting with a .335 average before finally getting his long-overdue call to Boston, where he'd go on to win five batting titles and earn a spot in the Hall of Fame.

He reassembled five of the original ECL franchises and launched a brand-new league, the American Negro League, with Hilldale as the cornerstone. To stock the club, he built the highest-salaried roster in franchise history with four future Hall of Famers on the same team: Oscar Charleston, Martin Dihigo, Biz Mackey, and Judy Johnson. The league lasted one season. The jerseys lasted longer.

Made with authentic wool baseball flannel and felt appliqué lettering, this jersey honors the 1929 Hilldale Giants team, a roster stacked with history-book names.

Special ground rules were put in place due to the right field corner being only 225 feet from home plate. The US was declared the winner after six innings by a score of 11-5. The attendance of 86,245 fans was considered the largest audience for a baseball game in history to date.

Despite financial issues, the Carp played in Hiroshima Municipal Stadium until 2008.

The club was bought by chewing gum magnate William Wrigley Jr. in 1921, who soon built the first Wrigley Field, a spectacular double-decked 21,000 seat ballpark at 42nd and Avalon. In 1958, they were forced to move to a smaller market as a result of the Brooklyn Dodgers' move to Los Angeles, which brought Major League Baseball competition into the PCL's territory. The franchise relocated to Spokane, Washington, as the Spokane Indians. 

Made from light-wash denim with our signature green satin underbrim and finished with a felt patch of their 1942 drop-shadow logo, this ballcap honors the Los Angeles Angels of the PCL.

body_html:
DENIM BALLCAP HONORING THE 1961 KANSAS CITY KATZ

History: Japan's second-largest city is home to one of its oldest professional baseball franchises: the Osaka Tigers, who first took the field in 1936. Their park, Koshien Field, is the oldest in Japan and is considered sacred ground by players and fans. There is also a statue of Babe Ruth outside the ballpark to commemorate the Bambino's 1934 visit to Osaka.

Made from mid-wash denim with our signature green satin underbrim and finished with an embroidered felt patch, this ballcap honors the Osaka Tigers.

title: San Francisco Seals Indigo Cotton Denim Ballcap
body_html:
DENIM BALLCAP HONORING THE 1940 SAN FRANCISCO SEALS

History: A charter member of the famed Pacific Coast League, the San Francisco Seals are one of the most recognizable minor league teams of all time. They were connected to all of the biggest teams in baseball, having been affiliated with the Yankees, Red Sox, Dodgers, and Giants at one time or another across their 54 year history. This design was worn by the 1940 Seals and Lefty O’Doul, who ended his career with a .349 career batting average and somehow never made the Hall of Fame.

Made from mid-wash denim with our signature green satin underbrim and finished with the 1940 team's iconic orange felt seal logo, this ballcap honors the San Francisco Seals.

title: New York Brooklyn Eagles Indigo Cotton Denim Ballcap
body_html:
DENIM BALLCAP HONORING THE BROOKLYN EAGLES

History: The Eagles played their inaugural season at Brooklyn’s Ebbets Field in 1935, but moved to Newark just one year later. Co-owned and managed by Effa Manley, the first and only woman inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame, the Eagles were a powerhouse of the Negro Leagues, winning the NLWS in 1946. The following year, their home-grown star Larry Doby became the second Black player to break the color barrier and the first in the American League.

Made from light wash denim with our signature green satin underbrim and a felt appliqué logo, this ballcap honors the historic Brooklyn Eagles.

title: Brooklyn Bushwicks Indigo Cotton Denim Ballcap
body_html:
DENIM BALLCAP HONORING THE 1949 BROOKLYN BUSHWICKS

History: For nearly four decades, the Brooklyn Bushwicks were the best semi-pro baseball team in New York — maybe in the country. They packed 15,000 fans into Dexter Park on Sunday afternoons, outdrew big-league franchises like the Phillies and the Boston Braves, and won four straight Inter-American Series titles from 1946 to 1949, where they represented the United States against the champions of Venezuela, Cuba, and Mexico. Then television arrived, Jackie Robinson integrated the majors, the Negro League opponents they'd barnstormed with disappeared, and the money dried up. The Bushwicks folded after 1951.

Made from dark wash denim with our signature green satin underbrim and featuring the Bushwicks 'B' in white felt appliqué, this ballcap pays tribute to a foundational team that played a stone’s throw from our namesake.

title: Kansas City Monarchs Indigo Cotton Denim Ballcap
body_html:
WOOL BALLCAP WORN BY THE 1945 KANSAS CITY MONARCHS

History: One of the most renowned Negro Leagues teams of all time, the Kansas City Monarchs produced fourteen Hall of Famers, from Bullet Rogan in the 1920s to Ernie Banks in the early 1950s. Made up of players from the All Nations barnstorming team and the Army’s 25th Infantry Wreckers, the Monarchs got their start in 1920 and played through 1965. The 1945 squad included Satchel Paige and Jackie Robinson in his professional debut, who hit over .370 during the season before signing with Brooklyn. 

Made from dark wash denim and featuring our signature green satin underbrim, this ballcap takes inspiration from the original on-field ballcap of the 1940 Kansas City Monarchs with their 'KC' logo applied with a felt patch.

title: Fuji Athletic Club Indigo Cotton Denim Ballcap
body_html:
DENIM BALLCAP HONORING THE PORTLAND FUJI

History: The Portland Fuji was coached by Frank Fukuda, who was fundamental in developing Japanese Baseball in the Pacific Northwest. Fukuda played, coached, and managed for the Seattle Asahi and other local ball clubs for nearly two decades. He moved to Portland in 1927, where he continued to lead teams like the Fuji to league and tournament championships.

Made from dark wash denim and featuring our signature green satin underbrim, this ballcap takes inspiration from the original 1931 Fuji Athletic Club ballcap with their white felt “Fuji” logo.

title: New York Black Yankees Indigo Cotton Denim Ballcap
body_html:
DENIM BALLCAP HONORING THE NEW YORK BLACK YANKEES

History: Originally named the Harlem Stars, the New York Black Yankees were founded in the summer of 1932. They spent their first years barnstorming across the country, sometimes playing doubleheaders in different states on successive days. They officially joined the Negro National League in 1936, where they played until their final season in 1948. Hall of Famer Satchel Paige had a stint with the Black Yankees, and other notable players from the team include “Fats” Jenkins, Ted “Double Duty” Radcliffe, and “Mule” Suttles.

Made from dark wash denim and featuring our signature green satin underbrim, this ballcap honors the New York Black Yankees with a felt appliqué of their logo.

title: Hilldale Athletic Club 1924 V-Neck Mesh Jersey
body_html:
V-NECK MESH JERSEY HONORING THE 1924 HILLDALE TEAM

History: In 1924, the best team in the Eastern Colored League was a Darby, Pennsylvania club called Hilldale — which had grown from a sandlot boys team into a genuine powerhouse under owner Ed Bolden. That fall, they faced the Kansas City Monarchs in the first-ever Colored World Series, playing nine games across a grueling back-and-forth series. Hilldale lost five games to four, and spent the whole next season itching for a rematch. They got what they wished for. Hilldale came back the very next year and beat the Monarchs to clinch the 1925 championship — just like you’d write it in a Hollywood script.

Made from lightweight, breathable knit mesh with a tackle twill appliqué of Hilldale's 1924 script, this jersey honors a powerhouse of the Negro Leagues built from a sandlot squad.

He'd already built one champion from the ground up with Hilldale, and he wasted no time doing it again. Within a year, the Stars joined the Negro National League and won the pennant in their very first season. Bolden ran the club until his death in 1950, building one of the city's proudest sports institutions out of pure conviction and grit.

Made with cotton twill and our signature green satin underbrim, this ballcap features a felt appliqué of the Philadelphia Stars logo in honor of the iconic Negro League ballclub.

History: The 100th Infantry team consisted of Japanese-American players from Hawaii. After the Empire of Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the U.S. government rounded up Japanese-American citizens and sent them to internment camps. However, the soldiers of the 100th infantry were granted an opportunity to “prove their patriotism.” But rather than allow them to stay in Hawaii, they were sent to Camp McCoy in Wisconsin. There they played baseball with other Camp McCoy personnel, but soon founded their own club, which they called the Aloha Team, with an emphasis on their Hawaiian — rather than Japanese — identity.

Made from lightweight, breathable knit mesh with tackle twill appliqué lettering, this jersey pays homage to the logo used by the Aloha during their days in Wisconsin.

In 1971, "Coach Les" took over Hawaii's baseball program with no scholarships, no field, and no budget for uniforms — so he borrowed some spare jerseys from a league team he also coached, which were green and orange. Murakami went on to build a national power from scratch: carving a stadium out of a rock quarry, leading the Rainbows to the 1980 College World Series, and sending dozens of players on to pro ball. He retired in 2000 after a 30-year career, but the orange lives on.

Made from lightweight, breathable knit mesh with tackle twill appliqué lettering, this jersey honors the University of Hawaii baseball program and the coach who built it, quite literally, from the dirt up.

title: Wade Boggs Hall of Fame T-Shirt
body_html: History: Wade Boggs began an 18-year Big League career in 1982 with the Boston Red Sox. His hitting was a particular calling card, winning eight Silver Slugger Awards and five American League batting titles. The first of his batting titles came in 1983, the start of a seven-season stretch in which he had at least 200 hits each season, an American League record that has only since been bested by Ichiro Suzuki. Following a down year in 1992 Boggs left the Red Sox and joined their rivals, the New York Yankees. He went on to record four straight seasons with a batting average of .300 or better and won two Gold Glove awards. He helped the Yankees to win the 1996 World Series against the Atlanta Braves, his only World Series title. He played a pivotal role in Game 6 of the series, drawing a bases-loaded walk as a pinch hitter in the 10th inning to force the go-ahead run before they ultimately won 8-6 and clinched the series, and Boggs famously celebrated by jumping on the back of a NYPD police horse and riding it around the field. Boggs spent 1998 and ’99, the final two seasons of his career, with the Tampa Bay Devil Rays. While with the Devil Rays he recorded his 3,000th hit, and became the first player in history to hit a home run for their 3,000th hit. Boggs was inducted into the Hall of Fame on his first ballot in 2005. The number 26 he wore with the Red Sox was retired by Boston, and the Devil Rays retired his number 12 jersey.

League: Puerto Rican League

History: For the 1954-1955 winter league season in Puerto Rico, the Cangrejeros boasted one of the greatest outfields in baseball history. In right was a 20-year-old Roberto Clemente, soon to make his debut with the Pittsburgh Pirates. In center was reigning National League MVP Willie Mays, who won the Puerto Rican MVP award. And in left was Puerto Rican star Luis Olmo. Nicknamed the "Panic Squad", the team won both the Puerto Rican League and Caribbean Series titles.

On September 30, 1972 Roberto Clemente became just the 11th player to record 3,000 hits when he hit a double against the New York Mets in what proved to be his final regular season at-bat. He made one more regular season appearance, his 2,433rd as a Pirate, on October 3 to tie Honus Wagner’s record for most games played for the team. Clemente passed away tragically on December 31 of that year. Attempting to provide aid and relief following a massive earthquake in Nicaragua, Clemente was in a plane that crashed just off the coast of Isla Verde, Puerto Rico. Following his sudden death, Clemente was elected into the Baseball Hall of Fame through a special election on March 20, 1973. His famous number, 21, was retired by the Pirates that same year.

History: Just after basketball was invented in 1891, teams were called “fives” in reference to their starting five players. The sport, like society, was racially segregated, and all-Black squads were called “colored quints,” “Negro cagers,” or “Black fives."

The sport remained divided from 1904 - when basketball was first introduced to African Americans on a wide-scale organized basis - until the racial integration of the National Basketball League in the 1940s and the National Basketball Association in 1950.

During that time, dozens of all-Black teams emerged, flourished, and excelled, staging culturally rich, socially meaningful events that strengthened Black communities in the face of Jim Crow oppression.
